This report inventories the pooled Down syndrome vocabulary data before any modelling: how much data each contributing study provides, over what ages, and how words understood, spoken and signed are distributed. It is deliberately separate from the [modelling report](../report/) and the [model pages](../models/) — a plain description of what we are fitting to.

Each row of the source data is one **parent-report checklist administration** for one child at one age: counts of words *understood* and *spoken* (and, for the signing sub-set, words *signed*), harmonised onto the common 800-item reference inventory. Children measured repeatedly contribute several rows, so observations exceed children. The current pooled sample comprises **1,078 observations of 576 children across eleven international studies, spanning ages 8–115 months** — 818 observations record words understood, 1,063 words spoken, and 528 words signed. Per-study detail is in @tbl-inventory; the figures then plot the raw observations, one colour per study.

## Study inventory

```{python}
#| label: tbl-inventory
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Per-study data inventory (observed counts). Obs. = checklist administrations; Children = distinct subjects; medians are of the observed word counts (blank where a study records no such measure)."
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

_p = Path("figures/dataset_summary_ds.csv")
if not _p.exists():
    _out = pd.DataFrame({"note": ["Run scripts/generate_descriptive_report.py first."]})
else:
    _d = pd.read_csv(_p)

    def _rng(lo, hi):
        return f"{int(round(lo))}–{int(round(hi))}"

    def _med(v):
        return "" if pd.isna(v) else f"{v:.0f}"

    _out = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "Study": _d["study"],
            "Obs.": _d["n_observations"].astype(int),
            "Children": _d["n_subjects"].astype(int),
            "Age (mo)": [_rng(a, b) for a, b in zip(_d["age_min"], _d["age_max"])],
            "Understood n": _d["understood_n"].astype("Int64"),
            "Understood med.": _d["understood_median"].map(_med),
            "Spoken n": _d["spoken_n"].astype("Int64"),
            "Spoken med.": _d["spoken_median"].map(_med),
            "Signed n": _d["signed_n"].astype("Int64"),
        }
    )
    _total = {
        "Study": "All",
        "Obs.": int(_d["n_observations"].sum()),
        "Children": int(_d["n_subjects"].sum()),
        "Age (mo)": _rng(_d["age_min"].min(), _d["age_max"].max()),
        "Understood n": int(_d["understood_n"].sum()),
        "Understood med.": "",
        "Spoken n": int(_d["spoken_n"].sum()),
        "Spoken med.": "",
        "Signed n": int(_d["signed_n"].sum()),
    }
    _out = pd.concat([_out, pd.DataFrame([_total])], ignore_index=True)
_out
```

The studies vary widely in size (from a dozen to a couple of hundred observations) and in the ages they cover: some are infant/toddler samples, others reach well into childhood. This heterogeneity is exactly why the models use study-level random effects.

## Vocabulary by age

Both receptive and expressive vocabulary rise with age, but with very wide between-child spread at every age — the raw scatter makes the case for a flexible (nonparametric) mean function and for modelling the between-child variability explicitly rather than assuming a tight growth curve.

![Words understood by age, coloured by study](figures/scatter_age_understood_ds.png){#fig-understood-age .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Words spoken by age, coloured by study](figures/scatter_age_spoken_ds.png){#fig-spoken-age .lightbox fig-align="left"}

## Words understood versus words spoken

Plotting spoken against understood shows the two are strongly coupled, and that observations sit largely **on or below the diagonal**: children generally say no more than they understand, and usually fewer. This comprehension-leads-production gap is the relationship the joint models formalise as the production ratio $q = P(\text{speak} \mid \text{understand})$.

![Words understood versus words spoken, coloured by study](figures/scatter_understood_spoken_ds.png){#fig-us .lightbox fig-align="left"}

## Signed vocabulary

Only a subset of studies record signed vocabulary. Where they do, signing is most visible in the early years — an alternative expressive route while spoken vocabulary is still emerging — motivating the signing models (VG14/VG15).

![Words signed by age (signing sub-set), coloured by study](figures/scatter_age_signed_ds.png){#fig-signed-age .lightbox fig-align="left"}

## Reading

The descriptive picture sets up the modelling: vocabulary grows with age but with large, study- and child-level variability; production trails comprehension; and signing contributes early expressive vocabulary in the studies that record it. The fitted models quantify each of these — see the [modelling report](../report/) and the [per-model pages](../models/).
